questions.explanation: This is Kyosoku Chapter 1 Section 1 items 2(1) and 2(2). Taking care that other people can travel safely is also a social responsibility of a driver and of a pedestrian.
questions.question: When using the road it is important not to think only of your own convenience, but to watch the movements of the pedestrians and vehicles around you and to travel with consideration for the other person's position.

questions.explanation: The traffic rules are the common promises everyone must keep so that all road users can travel safely and smoothly. Confident or not, keeping the traffic rules is a basic duty of a member of society (Kyosoku Chapter 1 Section 1 item 1).
questions.question: When you are confident of your driving and judge for yourself that there is no risk of causing a traffic accident, you need not follow the traffic rules.

questions.explanation: Proceeding slowly is not enough. The vehicle must come to a complete stop (一時停止) at the stopping position and check that it is safe before going on (Kyosoku Appendix 1(1)).
questions.question: Where a traffic light is showing a flashing red light, a vehicle may simply proceed slowly (徐行) past it.

questions.explanation: This is Kyosoku Appendix 1(1). A pedestrian may proceed while paying attention to other traffic, but vehicles and streetcars (trams) have a duty to stop.
questions.question: Where a traffic light is showing a flashing red light, a vehicle must come to a complete stop (一時停止) at the stopping position and check that it is safe before going on.

questions.explanation: Only vehicles and streetcars (trams) have a duty to stop. A pedestrian may proceed while paying attention to other traffic (Kyosoku Appendix 1(1)).
questions.question: Where a traffic light is showing a flashing red light, pedestrians as well as vehicles must come to a complete stop (一時停止) at the stopping position.

questions.explanation: This is Kyosoku Appendix 1(1). A flashing yellow light means that pedestrians, vehicles and streetcars (trams) alike may proceed while paying attention to other traffic.
questions.question: Where a traffic light is showing a flashing yellow light, a vehicle may proceed while paying attention to the traffic around it.

questions.explanation: It is the flashing red light that requires a stop. A flashing yellow light means you may proceed while paying attention to other traffic (Kyosoku Appendix 1(1)).
questions.question: Where a traffic light is showing a flashing yellow light, a vehicle must come to a complete stop (一時停止) at the stopping position.

questions.explanation: This is Kyosoku Appendix 1(1). On a green arrow light pointing right, a light road vehicle (bicycle, cart, etc.), a specified small motorized bicycle and a moped turning right by the two-step method may not proceed.
questions.question: While this signal is shown, an ordinary motor vehicle may proceed in the direction of the arrow even though the light ahead is red, but a general motorized bicycle (moped) that turns right by the two-step method may not.

questions.explanation: This is Kyosoku Appendix 1(3) part A. Whether the arms are raised out horizontally or raised vertically, traffic crossing the front of the officer's body is under the same meaning as a red light.
questions.question: In both of the hand signals shown, traffic heading towards the front of the officer's body is under the same meaning as a red light.

questions.explanation: This is Kyosoku Appendix 1(3) part A. Because it means the same as a yellow light, a vehicle that is already close to the stopping position and cannot stop safely may go on.
questions.question: While a police officer holds an arm raised vertically, a vehicle coming from the direction parallel to the front of the officer's body is under the same meaning as a yellow light, so it must stop at the stopping position if it can do so safely.

questions.explanation: This is Kyosoku Appendix 1(3) part A. For traffic parallel to the front of the officer's body it means the same as a yellow light.
questions.question: While a police officer holds an arm raised vertically, traffic crossing the front of that officer's body is under the same meaning as a red light.

questions.explanation: For crossing traffic it means the same as a red light. It is traffic parallel to the front of the officer's body that is under the same meaning as a yellow light (Kyosoku Appendix 1(3) part A).
questions.question: For a vehicle approaching the intersection from the direction that crosses the front of the body of a police officer who is controlling traffic with an arm raised vertically, this hand signal means the same as a yellow light.

questions.explanation: This is the note to Kyosoku Appendix 1(3) part A. Anywhere else, the stopping position for a hand signal is the same as for a traffic light.
questions.question: Where a police officer gives a hand signal at a place that is not an intersection and has no pedestrian crossing, bicycle crossing zone or railway crossing, a vehicle stops 1 metre in front of that officer.

questions.explanation: Not 3 metres but 1 metre in front (note to Kyosoku Appendix 1(3) part A).
questions.question: On a road that is not an intersection and has no pedestrian crossing, bicycle crossing or railway crossing, when stopping for a police officer's hand signal the driver need only stop 3 metres in front of that officer.

questions.explanation: This is Kyosoku Chapter 1 Section 4 item 1(8). Dangerous acts of this kind must not be done on the road.
questions.question: You must not sprinkle water on the road when the surface is liable to freeze.

questions.explanation: This is Kyosoku Chapter 1 Section 4 item 1(1). The road is a place where many people and vehicles travel, so dangerous acts that obstruct traffic must not be done.
questions.question: Dangerous acts that obstruct traffic must not be done on the road, and staggering about drunk, sitting down in the roadway or lying down in it count as such acts.

questions.explanation: However small the amount, cigarette ends, scraps of paper, empty cans and the like must not be thrown out of a vehicle (Kyosoku Chapter 1 Section 4 item 1(5)). The same applies to putting your body or an object out of the vehicle.
questions.question: Throwing scraps of paper or cigarette ends out of a vehicle is all right as long as the amount is small and it does not obstruct traffic.

questions.explanation: The sidewalk is part of the road too, so goods and the like must not be displayed on the road (Kyosoku Chapter 1 Section 4 item 2). The same applies to leaving earth, timber and other things that obstruct traffic.
questions.question: On a road where the sidewalk is separated from the roadway it does not obstruct vehicles, so goods may be displayed on the sidewalk.

questions.explanation: Playing catch, roller skating and the like must not be done where traffic is heavy (Kyosoku Chapter 1 Section 4 item 1(2)). Dangerous acts of this kind on the road obstruct traffic and cause accidents.
questions.question: On a road with heavy vehicle traffic, I stood facing a neighbourhood child and played at throwing a ball back and forth.

questions.explanation: This is Kyosoku Chapter 11 Section 1 item 5. Lending a car to someone who has been drinking counts as supplying a vehicle to a person likely to drive under the influence of alcohol, and it is prohibited (Road Traffic Act Article 65(2)).
questions.question: If a person who has been drinking may be about to drive, you must not lend that person your car.

questions.explanation: This is Kyosoku Chapter 11 Section 1 item 4. Kyosoku Chapter 1 Section 1 item 2(3) likewise lists taking out motor insurance against the worst as one of the attitudes a road user should hold.
questions.question: On top of the compulsory liability insurance or the mutual-aid scheme, it is wise to take out ordinary voluntary insurance as well, in case the worst happens.

questions.explanation: This is Kyosoku Chapter 4 Section 1 item 4. Even if you drank the night before, you may still be under the influence of alcohol when you drive the next morning.
questions.question: Even several hours after drinking, alcohol may still be affecting you, so driving can still count as driving under the influence of alcohol.

questions.explanation: This is Kyosoku Chapter 4 Section 1 item 2. If you feel drowsy you should also rest promptly and drive on only once the drowsiness has gone.
questions.question: When your drive looks like it will be a long one, it is good to decide on your rest stops in advance and to stop the car for a break once every two hours.

questions.explanation: Being within its period of validity does not excuse you from keeping it in the vehicle. A valid vehicle inspection certificate and a valid compulsory liability insurance certificate (or mutual-aid certificate) must be kept in the vehicle you drive (Kyosoku Chapter 4 Section 1 item 1(1)(b)).
questions.question: As long as the compulsory liability insurance certificate is still within its period of validity, you may drive without keeping it in the vehicle.

questions.explanation: Lowering your speed does not restore scattered attention or weakened judgement. When you are tired you should refrain from driving or drive only after your condition has improved, and in a state of extreme fatigue you must not drive at all (Kyosoku Chapter 4 Section 1 item 3).
questions.question: Even when you are tired, there is no problem in driving as long as you keep your speed down.

questions.explanation: Once drowsiness has set in, you must not drive. When you have taken cold or headache medicine that causes drowsiness, the rule is not to drive (Kyosoku Chapter 4 Section 1 item 3).
questions.question: Drowsiness set in after taking cold medicine, but because the errand was urgent, the driver drove anyway.

questions.explanation: That is the wrong place to keep them. These papers must be kept in the vehicle you drive (Kyosoku Chapter 4 Section 1 item 1(1)(b)).
questions.question: The vehicle inspection certificate and the compulsory liability insurance certificate are important papers, so it is enough to keep them at home rather than in the vehicle.

questions.explanation: This is the table in Kyosoku Chapter 4 Section 2 item 2. Riding a regular motorcycle or driving a large-sized special motor vehicle requires its own separate licence.
questions.question: A person who holds only a regular motor vehicle license is not driving without a license if, besides an ordinary motor vehicle, they drive a small-sized special motor vehicle or a general motorized bicycle (moped).

questions.explanation: This is Kyosoku Chapter 4 Section 2 item 3. You do not need a towing license to tow a vehicle whose gross vehicle weight is 750 kilograms or less either.
questions.question: When you tow a broken-down vehicle with a rope or a crane, you do not need a towing license.

questions.explanation: This is Road Traffic Act Article 87(1). The permit has to match the vehicle: an ordinary-vehicle learner's permit for an ordinary motor vehicle, a semi-medium-vehicle learner's permit for a semi-medium-sized motor vehicle, and so on.
questions.question: If you drive a large-sized, medium-sized, semi-medium-sized or ordinary motor vehicle for practice or for a test without holding the Class 1 or Class 2 driver's license for that vehicle, you must hold the learner's permit (仮免) that matches that type of vehicle.

questions.explanation: The conditions written on the licence must be observed (Kyosoku Chapter 4 Section 1 item 1(1)(c); Road Traffic Act Article 91). A large motorcycle license covers large motorcycles, regular motorcycles, small-sized special motor vehicles and general motorized bicycles (mopeds), but with this condition the two-wheelers are limited to automatic transmission vehicles (AT).
questions.question: With a large motorcycle license carrying an automatic-transmission-only condition, you may not ride a large motorcycle that needs clutch operation.

questions.explanation: It can be revoked. Where the holder of a learner's permit commits an offence in the driving of a motor vehicle, the Public Safety Commission may revoke that permit (Road Traffic Act Article 106-2(1) and Article 103(1)(v)).
questions.question: Because a learner's permit (仮免) is a licence for practice, it is never revoked even if the holder commits an offence or causes an accident.

questions.explanation: It does. A regular motor vehicle license covers ordinary motor vehicles, small-sized special motor vehicles and general motorized bicycles (mopeds) (Kyosoku Chapter 4 Section 2 item 2).
questions.question: A regular motor vehicle license does not let you drive a small-sized special motor vehicle.

questions.explanation: This is the note to the table in Kyosoku Chapter 4 Section 4 item 1. Children under 12 are counted three for two.
questions.question: When working out the seating capacity, three children under 12 are counted as two adults.

questions.explanation: This is Kyosoku Chapter 5 Section 1 item 5(3). Moving off in reverse is dangerous, so when you put the car into a garage, back it in beforehand so that you can drive out forwards.
questions.question: When you have no choice but to move off in reverse, and the view behind is poor or you are coming out of a narrow road onto a wide one, it is a good idea to have a passenger help you check behind.

questions.explanation: This is Kyosoku Chapter 5 Section 1 item 2(4). Using a phone while the vehicle is moving leaves too little attention for the traffic around you, so you prepare the phone beforehand so that it stays silent.
questions.question: Before you drive, it is a good idea to switch your mobile phone off or set it to drive mode so that it does not ring while you are driving.

questions.explanation: This is Kyosoku Chapter 5 Section 1 item 2(4). Using a radio-telephone device that has to be held in the hand is prohibited except while the vehicle is stopped (Road Traffic Act Article 71 item 5-5).
questions.question: While you are driving, except when the vehicle is stopped, you must not hold a mobile phone in your hand to talk on it, nor gaze at the screen of a car navigation device.

questions.explanation: This is Kyosoku Chapter 5 Section 1 item 2(1). The seat back is set so that your elbows are slightly bent when both hands are on the steering wheel.
questions.question: The fore-and-aft position of the seat should be set so that your knee is slightly bent when the clutch pedal is pressed right down.

questions.explanation: You must not gaze at the screen while the vehicle is moving. To check the route, stop in a safe place first and look then (Kyosoku Chapter 5 Section 1 item 2(4)).
questions.question: Having lost the way, the driver kept looking at the car navigation screen to check the route while still driving.

questions.explanation: One child seat is not enough. Every infant you carry must be in a child seat (Kyosoku Chapter 5 Section 1 item 4(1), Road Traffic Act Article 71-3 paragraph 3).
questions.question: When you carry two infants, it is enough to put one of them in a child seat and let the other wear only a seat belt.

questions.explanation: Where you might end up stopped in that part, you must not enter even on a green light. Wait before the marking (Kyosoku Chapter 5 Section 2 item 2(9)).
questions.question: The traffic ahead was congested and you were about to end up stopped inside a No stopping zone marking, but since the light was green you went on.

questions.explanation: This is Kyosoku Chapter 5 Section 2 item 1. Where there is a center line, the part where that line is drawn counts as the middle of the road, so it is not necessarily the middle of the road's width (Road Traffic Act Article 17 paragraph 4).
questions.question: A center line is sometimes drawn away from the middle of the road, and on such a road a vehicle must travel on the left of that center line.

questions.explanation: This is Kyosoku Chapter 5 Section 2 item 1. Even where moving out is allowed, such as when roadworks leave the left-hand side too narrow, you keep how far you move out small.
questions.question: When you are driving an ordinary motor vehicle and meet a situation in which you may move out onto the right-hand side of the road, the driver must keep the amount he moves out to the minimum needed, except where that road is one way.

questions.explanation: It is not in any circumstances. Where the road is one way, a vehicle may move out onto the right-hand side of the road (Kyosoku Chapter 5 Section 2 item 1(1)).
questions.question: A vehicle may never, in any circumstances, move out onto the right-hand side of the road, so it may not travel on the right-hand side even on a one-way road.

questions.explanation: It is not never allowed. When roadworks or the like leave the left-hand side too narrow to pass, a vehicle may move out onto the right-hand side (Kyosoku Chapter 5 Section 2 item 1(2)).
questions.question: Whatever the state of the road and whatever the other traffic, a vehicle is never allowed at all to move out onto the right-hand side of the road.

questions.explanation: It is not a duty. It means that on a one-way road a vehicle may also move out onto the right-hand side of the road (Kyosoku Chapter 5 Section 2 item 1(1)).
questions.question: On a one-way road, a vehicle must travel on the right-hand side of the road.

questions.explanation: This is Kyosoku Chapter 5 Section 3 item 1(2). What you must proceed slowly for is passing alongside a safety zone that has pedestrians on it.
questions.question: When passing alongside a safety zone with no pedestrians on it, a vehicle may go by without proceeding slowly (徐行).

questions.explanation: When there are no pedestrians you need not proceed slowly. What you must proceed slowly for is passing alongside a safety zone that has pedestrians on it (Kyosoku Chapter 5 Section 3 item 1(2)).
questions.question: Even when there is not a single person standing on a safety zone, a vehicle passing alongside it must proceed slowly (徐行).

questions.explanation: This is Kyosoku Chapter 5 Section 3 item 1(3). You may also proceed slowly past it when nobody is getting on or off and there is 1.5 metres or more between you and the streetcar.
questions.question: Even when passing a streetcar (tram) standing at a stop (bus stop, tram stop), a vehicle may proceed slowly (徐行) past it if there is a safety zone.

questions.explanation: There is no duty to wait. Where there is a safety zone, you may proceed slowly (徐行) past it (Kyosoku Chapter 5 Section 3 item 1(3)).
questions.question: Where a streetcar (tram) is standing at a stop (bus stop, tram stop) that has a safety zone, a vehicle must stop behind it and wait until nobody is getting on or off any more.

questions.explanation: This is Kyosoku Chapter 5 Section 3 item 6(2). As well as stopping, you must not obstruct the progress of pedestrians.
questions.question: When a driver crosses a side strip (路側帯) to enter a shop along the road, he must come to a complete stop (一時停止) just before crossing, even when no pedestrians are in sight.

questions.explanation: That is the braking distance. The reaction distance is the distance the vehicle travels from the moment the driver senses danger until the brakes actually begin to work (Kyosoku Chapter 5 Section 4 item 2(1)).
questions.question: The distance a vehicle covers from the moment the brakes begin to work until it has stopped completely is called the reaction distance.

questions.explanation: This is Kyosoku Chapter 5 Section 4 item 2(1). A vehicle cannot stop at once, so you drive at a speed at which you can still stop safely if danger arises, keeping this stopping distance in mind.
questions.question: The stopping distance a vehicle needs before it actually comes to rest is the length of the reaction distance plus the braking distance.

questions.explanation: That is the braking distance. The stopping distance is that braking distance plus the reaction distance (Kyosoku Chapter 5 Section 4 item 2(1)).
questions.question: Of the distance a vehicle travels before it stops, only the part after the brakes begin to work is called the stopping distance.

questions.explanation: The one that is an addition is the stopping distance, which is the reaction distance plus the braking distance. The braking distance is the distance from the moment the brakes begin to work until the vehicle stops (Kyosoku Chapter 5 Section 4 item 2(1)).
questions.question: The braking distance is the reaction distance and the stopping distance added together.

questions.explanation: That is the reaction distance. The braking distance is the distance from the moment the brakes begin to work until the vehicle stops (Kyosoku Chapter 5 Section 4 item 2(1)).
questions.question: The distance a vehicle runs on after the driver notices danger but before the brakes actually begin to work is called the braking distance.

questions.explanation: It changes with the state of the road surface. On a rain-wet road the braking distance grows longer even at the same speed (Kyosoku Chapter 5 Section 4 item 2(2)).
questions.question: As long as the speed is the same, the braking distance is the same whether or not the road surface is wet.

questions.explanation: This is Kyosoku Chapter 5 Section 5 item 1(5). You are obliged to sound it at a place with this sign, and at intersections with poor visibility and the like inside a section marked "Sound horn zone".
questions.question: When passing a place with a "Sound horn" road sign, a vehicle must sound its horn.

questions.explanation: Kyosoku Chapter 5, Section 5, item 2(2) forbids changing lanes across a yellow line, but that prohibition does not apply when you are giving way to an emergency vehicle (Road Traffic Act Article 26-2(3)(i)).
questions.question: Even on a road where the vehicle lanes are divided by a yellow line, when pulling over to the left-hand side of the road to give way to an emergency vehicle you may change lanes across that yellow line.

questions.explanation: This is Kyosoku Chapter 5 Section 5 item 1(1). When turning right or left somewhere other than an intersection, the signal likewise starts 30 metres before that point.
questions.question: When a vehicle turns right or left at an intersection, it must start the signal (by indicator or hand) on reaching the point 30 metres before that intersection.

questions.explanation: This is Kyosoku Chapter 5 Section 5 item 1(1). A U-turn sits in the same row of the table as a right turn, so both the timing and the method of the signal are the same as for a right turn.
questions.question: When a driver is going to make a U-turn part-way along a road, the moment to give the signal (by indicator or hand) is when the vehicle has come within 30 metres of the point where the turn is to begin.

questions.explanation: This is Kyosoku Chapter 5 Section 5 item 1(1). The figure of 30 metres before belongs to turning right or left and to a U-turn; changing lanes is about 3 seconds before.
questions.question: When changing lanes while travelling in the same direction, the signal (by indicator or hand) is given about 3 seconds before the change.

questions.explanation: That signal means a left turn or a change of course to the left. The signal for a right turn or a U-turn is made by putting the right arm out of the right side and stretching it horizontally, or by putting the left arm out of the left side and bending the elbow vertically upwards (Kyosoku Chapter 5 Section 5 item 1(1)).
questions.question: The figure shows the driver with the right arm out of the right side of the vehicle and the elbow bent vertically upwards. This signal (by indicator or hand) means a right turn or a U-turn.

questions.explanation: You do not speed up to get past first. When there is an obstacle in your path, you come to a complete stop (一時停止) or slow down beforehand and give way to the vehicle coming the other way (Kyosoku Chapter 5 Section 6 item 5(2)).
questions.question: When a works vehicle is standing in your path and an oncoming vehicle is approaching as well, it is best to speed up so as to get past before the oncoming vehicle.

questions.explanation: This is Kyosoku Chapter 5 Section 6 item 5(1). Whether you are passing close to a pedestrian or close to a bicycle, you must leave a safe gap or proceed slowly (徐行) (Kyosoku Chapter 5 Section 3 items 1(1) and 7(2)).
questions.question: When passing an oncoming vehicle, the driver must not only keep a safe gap from that vehicle but also pay attention to pedestrians and bicycles travelling on the left-hand side of the road.

questions.explanation: Where this yellow line is drawn, you may not cross into the right-hand side of the road to overtake, whether visibility is good or bad and whether or not there is an oncoming vehicle (Kyosoku Chapter 5 Section 6 item 1(4), Appendix 3(2) item 2).
questions.question: Even on a road with the yellow marking for No overtaking on the right-hand side of the road, a vehicle may cross into the right-hand side to overtake when visibility is good and there is no oncoming vehicle.

questions.explanation: This is Kyosoku Chapter 5 Section 6 item 1(3) part D. It is a tunnel without vehicle lanes that is a no-overtaking place; in a tunnel with vehicle lanes you may overtake unless something else forbids it.
questions.question: The inside of a tunnel that has vehicle lanes is not one of the places where overtaking is forbidden.

questions.explanation: The tunnel that is a no-overtaking place is a tunnel without vehicle lanes. A tunnel with vehicle lanes is not a no-overtaking place (Kyosoku Chapter 5 Section 6 item 1(3) part D).
questions.question: Inside a tunnel you may not change course to overtake a motor vehicle or pass along its side, whether or not the tunnel has vehicle lanes.

questions.explanation: On an upgrade it is the crest that is forbidden, and it is the downgrade that is forbidden for being steep. A steep upgrade in itself is not a no-overtaking place (Kyosoku Chapter 5 Section 6 item 1(3) part C).
questions.question: A steep upgrade is a place where overtaking is forbidden.

questions.explanation: This is Kyosoku Chapter 5, Section 7, item 2(6). You may also drive without following the designation when road works or the like leave you no choice.
questions.question: Even on a road where lanes are designated by direction of travel at an intersection by a road sign or a road marking, when an emergency vehicle approaches you may drive without following that designation.

questions.explanation: This is Kyosoku Chapter 5 Section 7 item 2(9). The same applies at a place with a "No stopping zone" road marking and at a railway crossing.
questions.question: Where traffic ahead is congested and going on would risk the vehicle becoming stuck on a pedestrian crossing, the vehicle must not enter the crossing.

questions.explanation: This is Kyosoku Chapter 5 Section 7 items 2(1) and 2(2). For a left turn you move over to the left edge of the road beforehand and follow the side of the intersection; for a right turn you move over towards the centre of the road beforehand and pass just inside the centre of the intersection.
questions.question: When a vehicle turns right or left at an intersection it must proceed slowly (徐行) as it goes through.

questions.explanation: Whether there are pedestrians makes no difference. When you turn right or left at an intersection you must proceed slowly as you go through (Kyosoku Chapter 5 Section 7 items 2(1) and 2(2)).
questions.question: When turning right or left at an intersection you need not proceed slowly (徐行) if there are no pedestrians crossing.

questions.explanation: Obeying the light makes no difference. To turn left you must move over to the left edge of the road beforehand and go slowly along the side of the intersection (Kyosoku Chapter 5 Section 7 item 2(1)).
questions.question: When you go on a green light you need not proceed slowly (徐行) even when turning left at the intersection.

questions.explanation: This is Kyosoku Chapter 5 Section 8 item 3(3). Two solid white lines mark a pedestrian-only side strip, which may not be entered regardless of its width.
questions.question: In a side strip (路側帯) marked with two solid white lines, a vehicle may not enter the strip to park, however wide it is.

questions.explanation: This is Kyosoku Appendix 3(1) item 54. It is an indication sign showing that a vehicle may stop.
questions.question: Where there is a "Stopping permitted" road sign, a vehicle may stop.

questions.explanation: A short time is no different. When you leave the vehicle you must stop the engine, apply the hand brake and take the key with you (Kyosoku Chapter 5 Section 8 item 10).
questions.question: If you will be back in a short time, you may leave the vehicle with the engine still running.

questions.explanation: This is Kyosoku Chapter 5 Section 9 item 1(2)(ii). Check the hand brake and the P position of the change lever before starting.
questions.question: When you start the engine of an automatic transmission vehicle (AT), you first check that the hand brake is on and the change lever is in P, then press the brake pedal and start it.

questions.explanation: Not N. You check that the hand brake is on and the change lever is in P, and then start the engine (Kyosoku Chapter 5 Section 9 item 1(2)(ii)).
questions.question: In an automatic transmission vehicle (AT) you may start the engine only when the hand brake is on and the change lever is in the N position.

questions.explanation: This is Kyosoku Chapter 5 Section 9 item 1(3). If you move the change lever without pressing the brake pedal firmly, the car may leap forward or suddenly reverse.
questions.question: The driver of an automatic transmission vehicle (AT) moves the change lever while keeping the brake pedal pressed firmly, checks with the eyes whether it is in D for forward or R for reverse, and only then moves off.

questions.explanation: This is Kyosoku Chapter 5 Section 9 item 1(3). The change lever goes to D to go forward and to R to reverse.
questions.question: To move off in an automatic transmission vehicle (AT), release the hand brake, let the brake pedal up gradually and press the accelerator pedal gently.

questions.explanation: Not P. R is for reversing, and P is for parking (Kyosoku Chapter 5 Section 9 items 1(3) and 1(5)).
questions.question: To reverse an automatic transmission vehicle (AT), you put the change lever in P.

questions.explanation: You do not keep the accelerator pedal pressed. While stopped, keep the brake pedal pressed firmly and put the hand brake on as well to be safe (Kyosoku Chapter 5 Section 9 item 1(4)).
questions.question: While an automatic transmission vehicle (AT) is stopped at an intersection, keeping the accelerator pedal pressed a little steadies the engine and is a good idea.

questions.explanation: This is Kyosoku Chapter 6 Section 1 item 1(5). At the same time, to avoid an engine stall, cross in one go without changing gear, staying in the low gear you moved off in.
questions.question: When you go across a railway crossing, keep a little towards the middle so as not to drop a wheel off the edge, while watching for pedestrians and oncoming vehicles.

questions.explanation: This is Kyosoku Chapter 6 Section 1 item 1(5). Keep a little towards the middle so as not to drop a wheel off the edge, while watching for pedestrians and oncoming vehicles.
questions.question: Once you have started across a railway crossing, it is best to cross in one go without changing gear, staying in the low gear you used to move off, so that the engine does not stall.

questions.explanation: You must not change gear. Inside a crossing you cross in one go without changing gear, staying in the low gear you moved off in, so that the engine does not stall (Kyosoku Chapter 6 Section 1 item 1(5)).
questions.question: Once you are in a railway crossing, you should change up to a higher gear at once and cross in one go.

questions.explanation: A pedestrian crossing is the same. Where congested traffic ahead means you might be unable to move on a pedestrian crossing or a railway crossing, you must not enter it (Kyosoku Chapter 5 Section 7 item 2(9)).
questions.question: When the traffic ahead is congested you must not enter a railway crossing, but ending up stopped on a pedestrian crossing cannot be helped.

questions.explanation: Just after it goes up is no different. Except at a crossing with a traffic light, you must stop just before the crossing, or just before the stop line where there is one, and check that it is safe to left and right with your own eyes and ears (Kyosoku Chapter 6 Section 1 item 1(1)).
questions.question: At a railway crossing where the barrier has just gone up, you may go across without coming to a complete stop (一時停止).

questions.explanation: Proceeding slowly is not enough. Except at a crossing with a traffic light, you must come to a complete stop (一時停止) just before the crossing and check that it is safe to left and right with your own eyes and ears, for instance by opening a window (Kyosoku Chapter 6 Section 1 item 1(1)).
questions.question: At a railway crossing with good visibility, you may cross if you proceed slowly (徐行) and check that it is safe to left and right.

questions.explanation: This is Kyosoku Chapter 6 Section 2 item 1(4). Using the foot brake too often on a long downhill can make the brakes suddenly stop working.
questions.question: On a downhill you use a low gear, in an automatic transmission vehicle (AT) by putting the change lever in 2 or L (or 1), and make good use of the engine brake.

questions.explanation: It is not without effect. In an automatic transmission vehicle you can make good use of the engine brake by putting the change lever in 2 or L (or 1) (Kyosoku Chapter 6 Section 2 item 1(4)).
questions.question: An automatic transmission vehicle (AT) gets no effect from the engine brake, so on a long downhill you slow down with the foot brake alone.

questions.explanation: This is Kyosoku Chapter 6 Section 2 item 1(6). Where there is a turnout nearby, the vehicle coming up may pull into it and wait instead.
questions.question: When passing an oncoming vehicle on a hill, because moving off on an upgrade is hard, the vehicle going down gives way to the vehicle coming up, except where there is a turnout nearby.

questions.explanation: This is Kyosoku Chapter 6 Section 2 item 1(8). On mountain roads the road shoulder is sometimes liable to crumble, so take care not to move too far onto it when passing an oncoming vehicle (Kyosoku Chapter 6 Section 2 item 1(9)).
questions.question: On a road with a cliff on one side from which a vehicle could fall, when an oncoming vehicle cannot be passed safely, the vehicle on the cliff side comes to a complete stop (一時停止) and gives way.

questions.explanation: This is Kyosoku Chapter 6 Section 2 item 1(4). On a long downgrade, using the brake pedal too often can make the brakes suddenly stop working, which is dangerous.
questions.question: When you drive down a long downgrade, it is best to select a low gear — in an automatic transmission vehicle (AT) by moving the change lever to 2 or L (or 1) — and to descend with the engine brake working.

questions.explanation: It is the other way round. Because moving off on an upgrade is hard, the vehicle going down gives way to the vehicle coming up. Where there is a turnout nearby, however, the vehicle coming up may pull into it and wait (Kyosoku Chapter 6 Section 2 item 1(6)).
questions.question: When passing an oncoming vehicle on a hill, the vehicle coming up must give way to the vehicle going down.

questions.explanation: This is Kyosoku Chapter 6 Section 3 item 1(4). The brake light is also the signal given when a driver is about to proceed slowly (徐行) or stop, so you must keep a following distance at which you would not run into the vehicle ahead if it stopped suddenly (Kyosoku Chapter 5 Section 4 item 2(4)).
questions.question: When following another vehicle at night, watch its brake light, and when the brake light comes on, judge that the vehicle ahead is pressing the brake pedal to slow down and keep a good distance behind it.

questions.explanation: A two-wheeled vehicle runs while the rider holds it steady with the body and loses its stability once it stops, a structural feature that calls for riding skills different from those of a four-wheeled vehicle. The rider must not let the machine's handiness breed carelessness and must ride carefully at all times (Kyosoku Chapter 8 Section 1).
questions.question: A two-wheeled vehicle (motorcycles and general motorized bicycles) is a handy machine and easy to operate, so it need not be ridden as carefully as a four-wheeled vehicle.

questions.explanation: This is Kyosoku Chapter 8 Section 3 item 3(2)イ. When the small right turn is used, the rider may turn right on a green arrow light.
questions.question: At an intersection on a road carrying the sign Right turn method for general motorized bicycles (small turn), and at other intersections where the two-step right turn does not apply, a general motorized bicycle (moped) must move over as close to the centre of the road as it can beforehand and turn right just inside the centre of the intersection, proceeding slowly (徐行).

questions.explanation: In the two-step right turn the rider moves over as close to the left edge of the road as possible beforehand, goes straight across to the far side of the intersection on a green light while proceeding slowly, stops there and turns to face right (Kyosoku Chapter 8 Section 3 item 3(2)ア). Moving over to the centre of the road is the small right turn.
questions.question: When a general motorized bicycle (moped) makes a two-step right turn, it too moves over as close to the centre of the road as it can beforehand and passes just inside the centre of the intersection, proceeding slowly (徐行), exactly as a motor vehicle does.

questions.explanation: The two-step right turn applies at intersections under traffic control by a traffic light or the like, on a road carrying the sign or on a road with three or more vehicle lanes (Kyosoku Chapter 8 Section 3 item 3(2)ア). At an intersection not under traffic control the rider makes a small right turn (Kyosoku Chapter 8 Section 3 item 3(2)イ).
questions.question: At an intersection where traffic is not under traffic control, a general motorized bicycle (moped) must make a two-step right turn.

questions.explanation: This is Kyosoku Chapter 8 Section 4 item 2(1). If the riding posture is not kept correct at that moment, the rider is thrown forward.
questions.question: When the rider of a two-wheeled vehicle (motorcycles and general motorized bicycles) applies the brakes, it is best to keep the machine standing straight without turning the handlebars and to use the front and rear brakes at the same time while letting the engine brake work.

questions.explanation: This is Kyosoku Chapter 8 Section 6 item 3. A machine whose engine is running, one that is towing another vehicle and one with a sidecar are not treated as a pedestrian when pushed.
questions.question: A person pushing a two-wheeled vehicle (motorcycles and general motorized bicycles) with the engine switched off is treated as a pedestrian and may use the sidewalk, but it is otherwise if what is being pushed is towing another vehicle or has a sidecar.

questions.explanation: A machine with a sidecar is not treated as a pedestrian when pushed, even with the engine switched off (Kyosoku Chapter 8 Section 6 item 3). What is treated as a pedestrian is pushing a two-wheeled vehicle whose engine is not running, which is not towing another vehicle and which has no sidecar.
questions.question: Even a two-wheeled vehicle (motorcycles and general motorized bicycles) with a sidecar is treated as a pedestrian while it is being pushed with the engine switched off.

questions.explanation: An offence or an accident brings criminal liability such as a fine or imprisonment, and administrative liability in the form of licence revocation or licence suspension (Road Traffic Act Article 103(1) and (2)). If someone is injured or property is damaged, there is also civil liability, namely compensating the victim for the loss.
questions.question: A driver who commits a traffic offence or causes a traffic accident may bear three kinds of liability: criminal, administrative and civil liability.

questions.explanation: Road Traffic Act Article 64(1) forbids driving and says this includes the case where the licence has been suspended. The opening passage of Kyosoku Chapter 4 Section 2 likewise states that a person under a licence suspension may not drive during that period.
questions.question: Even if you hold a licence, driving during a period when that licence is suspended counts as driving without a license.

questions.explanation: They may not. Driving during a period when the licence is suspended counts as driving without a license, whether or not the licence card is still in hand (Road Traffic Act Article 64(1); Kyosoku Chapter 4 Section 2 opening passage).
questions.question: A person under a licence suspension may drive during that period as long as the licence card has not been taken away.

questions.explanation: This is Kyosoku Appendix 3(2) item 1. Where a figure is added to the symbol, it shows the hours during which U-turns are forbidden.
questions.question: This road marking shows that vehicles are forbidden to make a U-turn.

questions.explanation: This marking shows the end of the section in which U-turns are forbidden, so beyond it you may make one (Kyosoku Appendix 3(2) item 24).
questions.question: Beyond this road marking you may not make a U-turn.

questions.explanation: This is Kyosoku Appendix 3(2) item 3. Where the lanes are divided by solid yellow lines on both sides, a vehicle in either lane may not change lanes.
questions.question: In the vehicle lanes divided by this road marking, you may change lanes neither from A to B nor from B to A.

questions.explanation: This is Kyosoku Appendix 3(2) item 3. What the marking in this figure forbids is a lane change by a vehicle in the lane on the solid-yellow-line side.
questions.question: On a road with this road marking, a vehicle in the lane on the broken-white-line side may change into the lane beside it.

questions.explanation: A vehicle in the lane on the broken-white-line side may change lanes. The one that may not is the vehicle in the lane on the solid-yellow-line side (Kyosoku Appendix 3(2) item 3).
questions.question: On a road with this road marking, even a vehicle in the lane on the broken-white-line side may not change into the lane beside it.

questions.explanation: This is Kyosoku Appendix 3(2) item 4. Even a brief stop to let someone in or out is not allowed.
questions.question: This road marking shows that both stopping and parking are forbidden.

questions.explanation: This marking gives advance warning that there is a pedestrian crossing or bicycle crossing ahead (Kyosoku Appendix 3(2) item 38). Except where it is clear that no pedestrian or bicycle is crossing, the driver must slow down enough to stop just before it (Kyosoku Chapter 5 Section 3 item 2(2)).
questions.question: When approaching a place where this road marking is laid, a vehicle may go on at the same speed if it is clear that no pedestrian or bicycle is crossing.

questions.explanation: This is Road closed, and pedestrians, remotely operated small vehicles, vehicles and streetcars (trams) alike may not pass (Kyosoku Appendix 3(1) item 1).
questions.question: This road sign forbids vehicles to pass, but pedestrians may.

questions.explanation: This is Kyosoku Appendix 3(1) item 2. Closed to vehicles applies to every vehicle, so light road vehicles such as bicycles may not pass either.
questions.question: On a road with this sign, not only motor vehicles but general motorized bicycles (mopeds) and light road vehicles as well may not pass.

questions.explanation: Closed to vehicles applies to every vehicle. Mopeds and light road vehicles may not pass either (Kyosoku Appendix 3(1) item 2).
questions.question: Someone riding a general motorized bicycle (moped) may enter and travel on the road where this sign stands.

questions.explanation: No vehicle of any kind may pass. Where the kinds are limited, that is shown by an auxiliary sign (Kyosoku Appendix 3(1) item 2).
questions.question: This sign shows that only ordinary motor vehicles may not pass.

questions.explanation: This is Closed to vehicles, and only vehicles are forbidden. The sign that forbids pedestrians as well is Road closed (Kyosoku Appendix 3(1) items 1 and 2).
questions.question: Where this sign stands, pedestrians may not pass either.

questions.explanation: That describes No entry for vehicles. This sign is Closed to vehicles: no vehicle may pass from either direction (Kyosoku Appendix 3(1) items 2 and 3).
questions.question: This sign is placed at the exit of a one-way street and the like, and shows that vehicles may not enter from that direction.

questions.explanation: This is the Stop sign. You must come to a complete stop (一時停止) just before the stop line, or just before the intersection where there is no stop line, and must not obstruct the progress of the vehicles and streetcars (trams) travelling on the crossing road (Kyosoku Chapter 5 Section 7 item 3(3), Appendix 3(1) item 40).
questions.question: At an intersection with this sign, you may go through proceeding slowly (徐行) if you can see clearly to left and right and it is obviously safe.
